updates.summary: A voluntary, ASEAN-endorsed guide for organisations that design, develop and deploy traditional AI in commercial and non-military or dual-use applications, aimed at alignment and interoperability across ASEAN. It sets seven guiding principles, including transparency and explainability, security and safety, human-centricity and accountability, and a governance framework: internal governance structures, risk impact assessments that set the level of human involvement (human-in-the-loop, over-the-loop or out-of-the-loop), operations management, and disclosure of AI use to stakeholders. It recommends national and regional measures, including an ASEAN Working Group on AI Governance.
updates.notes: Endorsed at the 4th ASEAN Digital Ministers' Meeting (ADGMIN) in Singapore on 1-2 February 2024, which also welcomed the recommendation to set up a Working Group on AI Governance under ADGSOM, including initial work on generative AI. Adoption is voluntary; the guide does not replace or supersede existing or upcoming laws and is meant to be a living document reviewed by ASEAN sectoral bodies. Annex A gives an AI risk impact assessment template and Annex B six use cases. Supplemented by the Expanded ASEAN Guide on AI Governance and Ethics – Generative AI (ASEAN-02), a separate publication rather than a new version of this guide.

updates.summary: India's national AI governance framework. It sets seven guiding principles or sutras (trust, people first, innovation over restraint, fairness and equity, accountability, understandable by design, and safety, resilience and sustainability) and recommendations across six pillars, including an India-specific risk assessment framework based on evidence of harm, a graded liability system, voluntary measures backed by techno-legal solutions, a national AI incident database, and new bodies: an AI Governance Group, a Technology & Policy Expert Committee and the AI Safety Institute. It finds that existing laws can address many risks and that a separate AI law is not needed at this stage.
updates.notes: A drafting committee constituted by MeitY in July 2025 and chaired by Prof. Balaraman Ravindran (IIT Madras) wrote the guidelines. It built on a draft report by a sub-committee on AI governance under the Principal Scientific Adviser's advisory group, which MeitY published for public feedback and which drew more than 2,500 submissions; that draft is superseded by these guidelines. The seven sutras are adapted from the Reserve Bank of India's FREE-AI Committee report. Principal Scientific Adviser Prof. Ajay Kumar Sood unveiled the guidelines on 5 Nov 2025, calling 'Do No Harm' the guiding principle of the framework, ahead of the India-AI Impact Summit (New Delhi, 19-20 Feb 2026). PIB published an explainer on 15 Feb 2026 for the Summit. India has no AI-specific statute.

updates.summary: Binding amendment to India's intermediary rules on 'synthetically generated information' (SGI): content artificially or algorithmically created or altered so that it appears real and depicts a person or event as indistinguishable from reality. Intermediaries offering SGI tools must use technical measures to block unlawful SGI, such as child sexual abuse material, non-consensual intimate imagery or deceptive depictions of real people or events, and must prominently label other SGI and embed permanent metadata or a unique identifier where feasible. Significant social media intermediaries must obtain and verify user declarations of SGI and label it.
updates.notes: G.S.R. 120(E) of 10 February 2026 amends the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 (G.S.R. 139(E) of 25 February 2021); the amendment came into force on 20 February 2026. Besides the SGI provisions, it clarifies that removing or disabling access to information, including SGI, in compliance with the rules does not breach the safe-harbour conditions of section 79(2) of the IT Act; requires intermediaries to inform users at least every three months of the consequences of non-compliance, and those offering SGI tools to warn users of penalties for misuse; and shortens deadlines: removal on a court order or a government authority's reasoned intimation from 36 to 3 hours (rule 3(1)(d) as substituted by G.S.R. 775(E) of 22 October 2025, in force from 15 November 2025), removal of intimate or impersonating imagery on complaint from 24 to 2 hours, grievance resolution from 15 to 7 days, and certain removal requests from 72 to 36 hours. A draft of the SGI amendment was published for consultation on 22 October 2025. The rules follow MeitY's non-binding AI advisories to intermediaries of 1 March 2024, revised on 15 March 2024 to drop a prior-approval requirement for under-tested models. On 30 March 2026 MeitY released a further draft amendment to the IT Rules, open for comment until 16 April 2026, under which intermediaries would have to comply with MeitY's clarifications, advisories, orders, directions, standard operating procedures and guidelines on implementing the rules as part of their due diligence.

updates.summary: Draft general statute on artificial intelligence that ETDA and the Ministry of Digital Economy and Society put to public hearing in July 2026. It would cover AI affecting people in Thailand, even from abroad, and require foreign providers to appoint a local coordinator or representative. It prohibits AI using subliminal techniques or causing unfair broad-scale discrimination and provides for designating high-risk AI, whose deployers must manage risk, keep logs and report unforeseen risks; royal decrees may require notification, registration or licensing. Public agencies need ethical impact assessments, AI output must be machine-detectable and labelled, and liability is strict.
updates.notes: Tilleke & Gibbins give 2 July 2026 as the release date and about 30 days as the hearing period; comments went to the Ministry of Digital Economy and Society. The draft follows ETDA's public hearing of 11 to 24 June 2025 on the '(Draft) Principles of the Law on Artificial Intelligence', which proposed risk-based supervision of high-risk AI, legal promotion measures such as text and data mining and a regulatory sandbox, and a role for sector regulators. Regulation would be decentralised: sector regulators supervise AI in their fields and propose to a national AI planning committee which systems should count as high-risk, designated by royal decree in areas such as national security, health, environment, energy, telecommunications, transport and public utilities. Exempt would be AI used by individuals for personal or household purposes, research by higher education institutions with ethics committee approval, research and development before distribution, and systems prescribed by royal decree. Public agencies would record their AI uses in a central registry. The committee could designate 'contract-controlled AI businesses' serving government or critical infrastructure agencies and require data processing in Thailand for AI of national importance. The draft also provides for court-ordered suspension, recall or blocking through internet service providers, administrative fines of THB 1 to 5 million, a regulatory sandbox, and industry self-regulation that the committee may endorse. Core measures on launching AI products would apply on publication, and risk-control, supervision and serious-incident provisions 180 days later. After the hearing the draft goes to the Office of the Council of State, the Cabinet and the House of Representatives; the government aimed to start the legislative process by September 2026.
